result.summary: The Argonauts reach the land of the Bebrycians, where Polydeuces kills King Amycus in a boxing match and the heroes rout his people. They sail on through the Bosporus to Phineus, the blind prophet tormented by the Harpies. The sons of Boreas drive the Harpies off, and Phineus foretells the dangers and the route ahead to Colchis.

scenes.title: Polydeuces boxes King Amycus
scenes.summary: Amycus demands that any stranger box with him. Polydeuces accepts, outfights him and kills him with a blow above the ear.
scenes.stakes: Polydeuces risks his life against a brutal king who has killed many strangers; the crew would be held until a champion won.

scenes.title: Rout of the Bebrycians
scenes.summary: The Bebrycians attack and are scattered by the heroes. Lycus and the Mariandyni ravage their land. The Argonauts feast, sing and sail on at dawn.
scenes.stakes: The Argonauts face a mass attack by the Bebrycians after their king's death.

scenes.title: Arrival at Phineus' home
scenes.summary: The Argo survives a great wave in the Bosporus and lands near Phineus. The blind old seer, punished by Zeus and plagued by the Harpies, comes out to meet them.
scenes.stakes: Phineus suffers starvation and torment; the crew risk a wave that threatens to destroy the ship.

scenes.title: Boreads chase the Harpies
scenes.summary: Phineus begs for help and the sons of Boreas agree after he swears an oath. They chase the Harpies, and Iris stops them with a pledge by the Styx.
scenes.stakes: Phineus faces perpetual starvation; the Boreads risk divine wrath if they kill the Harpies.

scenes.title: Phineus prophesies the voyage
scenes.summary: After a feast Phineus describes the Clashing Rocks and the coast route to Colchis and the grove of the fleece. Jason, dismayed, asks about the return.
scenes.stakes: The Argonauts risk destruction at the Clashing Rocks and in the long unknown voyage to Colchis.

alias_notes.explanation: Patronymic by his mortal foster-father; he is also called son of Zeus.
Epithet meaning god of birth or ancestor.
Phineus' 'son of Leto' is Phoebus Apollo, giver of prophecy.

notable_quotes.reason: Phineus insists his prophecy must be obeyed: what he foretells will come to pass.
Explains why prophecy is always incomplete: gods keep humans needing to seek their will.

analysis.text: Hospitality and arrogance are tested: Amycus abuses strangers and is destroyed, while Phineus, punished for revealing too much, is relieved by the heroes' help.
Phineus' catalogue of Black Sea peoples reflects Hellenistic geographical knowledge of the Pontic coast and colonisation routes.

legacy.text: The Clashing Rocks and the dove sent through them influenced later sea-voyage stories and the Greek tradition of the Symplegades.

fun_facts.text: The Cyanean rocks were later identified with islets near the Bosporus's entrance to the Black Sea.

language_notes.text: "Poseidon Genethlius" means Poseidon as god of birth or ancestry; "bare" is archaic for "bore", so Melie bore Amycus to Poseidon.
Bebrycians: a people of the region of Bithynia, on the coast of Asia Minor, ruled by Amycus.
"Thy" and "thou" are archaic singular forms of "your" and "you"; "hold now" means "stop" or "restrain yourself".
The mantle was a gift from a Lemnian woman, recalling the Argonauts' earlier stay on Lemnos, ruled by women.
Typhoeus (Typhon) was a monstrous giant who challenged Zeus; Earth bore giants in anger against Zeus. Amycus is likened to such monsters.
Gauntlets here are boxing thongs of rawhide wrapped around the hands and forearms, not armoured gloves.
Minyan heroes: the Argonauts, many of whom descended from the Minyans of Iolcus and Orchomenus.
"Not yet destined to an evil death" means Iphitus survives this fight; the poet hints he will die later, and Clytius is named as his eventual killer.
"Bethink ye" means "consider" or "just imagine."
"I ween" is archaic for "I think" or "I suppose."
"Beside the bowl" refers to the mixing bowl for wine; the heroes spent the night feasting and drinking rather than sleeping.
"The Therapnaean son of Zeus" is Polydeuces (Pollux), whose cult was at Therapne in Laconia. The crew sing in praise of him after his victory.
The wave 'sinks away into calm' for a skilled helmsman: the Argo is saved because Tiphys steers it so well that the wave collapses harmlessly.
Hawsers are thick ropes used to moor a ship; fastening them means the Argonauts tied the Argo to the shore.
Leto's son is Apollo, god of prophecy. He gave Phineus the gift of seeing the future, which later brought about his suffering.
Harpies are winged female monsters of Greek myth who snatch and defile food; here they torment Phineus.
An oracle had foretold that the arrival of a certain band of men would end his torment. This refers to the Argonauts, including the sons of Boreas, who later drive off the Harpies.
'Naught but the skill held his bones together' means he is so wasted that only his sinews and skin keep his skeleton intact.
Hellenes is the Greek name for the Greeks. The fleece is the Golden Fleece, the goal of the voyage.
The king, son of Leto, is Apollo, who gave Phineus prophecy. Phineus thanks him for sending the heroes.
Zeus as god of suppliants (Zeus Hikesios) protected those who begged for help. Phoebus is a title of Apollo.
The Fury setting her foot on his eyes means divine vengeance has blinded him.
Adamant is a legendary unbreakable hard substance, here used for a heart of utter hardness.
The Floating Islands are the Symplegades, clashing rocks the Argo must later pass. Here the passage gives an etymology for the name Islands of Turning.
An oath by the Styx, the river of the underworld, was the gods' most binding oath and could not be broken.
Minoan Crete means Crete, the island of King Minos.
Phineus was blinded and plagued by the Harpies for revealing too much of Zeus's plans; this is the folly he refers to.
The Cyanean rocks are the Symplegades, the Clashing Rocks at the Bosporus entrance to the Black Sea (Pontus).
"I ween" is archaic for "I think" or "I suppose".
Acheron is a river of the underworld; the cave near Acherusia was believed to be an entrance to Hades.
Pelops, the Eneteian hero, gave his name to the Peloponnese; the Paphlagonians claimed descent from him.
The Amazons are the legendary warrior women; the Chalybes were famed ancient ironworkers.
"Hellas" is Greece; "Pontus" is the Black Sea.

context_notes.text: Polydeuces (Pollux) and his brother Castor were the Dioscuri; Polydeuces was the great boxer, said to be a son of Zeus.
Polydeuces is called son of Tyndareus, his mortal stepfather, though sentence 14 calls him son of Zeus.
Ancaeus, an Arcadian, fights with an axe and wears a bearskin; the sons of Aeacus are Peleus and Telamon.
Lycus was king of the Mariandyni, friendly to the Argonauts, and used the Bebrycians' loss of their king to attack their old enemies.
Heracles had been left behind on the coast of Mysia while searching for Hylas, so he missed the boxing contest with Amycus.
Tiphys is the Argo's helmsman, famed for his skill at steering. His expertise has just saved the crew from the Clashing Rocks region's dangers.
Phineus was a Thracian king and seer in Bithynia, on the Bosporus coast. The Argonauts seek his advice on their route to Colchis.
Zeus punished Phineus for revealing the gods' plans too openly to mortals, a violation of the divine order.
The Harpies are winged female spirits of storm winds who snatch things away. Here they were sent to torment Phineus.
Boreas is the North Wind. His sons Zetes and Calais are winged heroes among the Argonauts and brothers of Phineus's wife Cleopatra.
Iris is the gods' rainbow messenger. She speaks for Zeus, whose hounds the Harpies are called.
Phineus, a blind prophet, had been starved by the Harpies, who snatched his food. The Argonauts are freeing him, hence his ravenous eating.
The sons of Boreas, Zetes and Calais, had gone to drive off the Harpies.
Aeetes is king of Colchis and keeper of the golden fleece, which Jason has come to take.

literary_notes.text: Amycus is likened to a wounded lion fixed on the one hunter who struck him, showing his dangerous, single-minded rage.
Amycus the earth-born monster is set against Polydeuces as a bright star, marking the moral and physical opposition of the fighters.
The narrator's remark that they bound the gauntlets "for the last time" announces Amycus's death before the fight proceeds.
Amycus's attack is compared to a wave against a ship, with Polydeuces as the skilled pilot who escapes the shock.
The shipwrights' hammering gives the sound of blows and cracking teeth, turning the fight into laborious craftsmanship.
The heroes are likened to wolves scattering sheep, making the Bebrycians seem helpless, panicked livestock rather than warriors.
Smoked-out bees stand for the Bebrycians driven from their position, buzzing and dazed; this follows the wolf simile with a different image of flight.
The narrator calls the fleeing Bebrycians fools for not seeing another disaster awaits them at home, which the reader is told before they learn it.
The speaker's wry wish that Heracles' club would have taught Amycus to forget the rules turns the king's own arrogance against him.
The remark that all this was by the counsel of Zeus hints that Heracles' absence belongs to a larger divine plan.
The wave is compared to a steep mountain and a cloud, stressing its size and menace before it suddenly subsides.
The Harpies leave Phineus just enough food to survive, so that he stays alive to suffer; his survival is itself part of the punishment.
Likening Phineus to a lifeless dream presents him as barely substantial, a ghostlike figure of extreme frailty.
The darkness, the reeling earth and the speechless collapse give a vivid physical sense of his weakness and prepare for his prophecy.
Phineus claims escaping one's own thoughts is easier than escaping the Harpies, stressing their impossible speed.
Phineus's solemn oath calling on his own blindness and curses shows his desperation and his piety toward the gods.
The Harpies are compared to blasts of wind and lightning, conveying sudden, violent speed.
The hounds that gnash their teeth just short of the prey mirror the brothers' near, futile grasp at the Harpies.
Phineus's feasting is compared to a dream, conveying his disbelief after long starvation.
The crashing rocks and boiling, roaring water make the danger vivid and sensory.
Even an iron Argo could not survive, stressing the rocks' overwhelming force.
Phineus's fatalistic assertion suggests that events are fixed and the warning must be heeded.
The sleepless dragon coiled over the fleece creates a menacing picture of the final goal.
Jason's anxious remark shows his dismay and his sense of inexperience as leader.
